_comment: Reading explanations written for this app (the released tests publish only the answer key). Keyed by question ID from src/data/deck.json.
naep-r061901: Vera, the niece, invents the tragedy of the open window, and nervous Framton flees in terror when the men walk in. The last line gives her away: “Romance at short notice was her specialty.” A gets the roles wrong—Mrs. Sappleton isn’t Framton’s aunt, and he hears the story rather than telling it.
naep-r061902: To be self-possessed is to be calm and in control of yourself. Vera chats easily with a stranger and keeps a straight face through her invented tale; the one moment her voice “lost its self-possessed note,” it became “falteringly human.” She is imaginative too, but that’s a different trait.
naep-r061903: Early on, Framton doubts these visits will help “the nerve cure which he was supposed to be undergoing,” and his sister warns that moping will make his “nerves” worse. Meeting her friends is something she arranged once he was going, not the reason he went. And Mrs. Sappleton is Vera’s aunt, not his.
naep-r061907: A delusion is a false belief. Framton assumes strangers are “hungry for the least detail” of his ailments, but Mrs. Sappleton answers in a voice that “only replaced a yawn at the last moment.” A is tempting because he does have nerve trouble, but the delusion is about other people’s interest, not his illness.
naep-r061911: Saki lets you believe Vera’s ghost story right along with Framton, then reveals the truth only in the last line: “Romance at short notice was her specialty.” D is tempting, but no one’s identity is disguised—the three men really are the husband and brothers. What’s hidden is that Vera’s story was false.
naep-r062901: The introduction calls the celebration “the largest and most diverse of any in memory,” then lists cowboys, American Indians, coal miners, soldiers, and students. Diverse means varied—a wide range of people. It never says the event was the first open to everyone or that the speech set a length record.
naep-r062904: Perils are dangers. Roosevelt says, “Our forefathers faced certain perils which we have outgrown”—dangers from the nation’s past—and contrasts them with “other perils” the founders couldn’t foresee. Population growth is mentioned nearby, but as a source of problems, not as the perils themselves.
naep-r062905: Formidable means hard and intimidating. Roosevelt says “never before” has anyone tried “so vast and formidable an experiment” as running a whole continent as a democracy. Something never tried before can’t be conventional, and “vast” already covers its size, so “formidable” adds the idea of difficulty.
naep-r062906: Roosevelt names it directly: “administering the affairs of a continent under the forms of a democratic republic”—democracy on a huge scale. He then warns that if it fails, “free self-government throughout the world” will suffer. Industrial growth appears in the same paragraph, but as a change that makes the experiment harder, not the experiment itself.
naep-r062907: Roosevelt says the nation’s growth “is inevitably accompanied by a like growth in the problems,” and that “Power invariably means both responsibility and danger.” Inevitably and invariably both mean it always happens: progress brings problems with it. B is tempting, but he never says progress solves problems—he says it creates new ones.
naep-r062910: The final sentence praises the qualities “which made great the men who founded this republic” under Washington and “preserved this republic” under Lincoln. Roosevelt recalls those past achievements to inspire listeners to show the same courage and devotion now. He says nothing about how those presidents spoke or how powerful government was.
naep-r013601: Mary tells Warren, “Surely you wouldn’t grudge the poor old man / Some humble way to save his self-respect” (lines 52–53). Offering to ditch the meadow lets Silas come home without admitting he needs charity. She doesn’t think Warren needs the help—she’s sure “His working days are done” (line 160).
naep-r013603: Mary hurries to meet Warren “with the news / And put him on his guard” (lines 4–5), tells him “Be kind” (line 7), and later hushes him: “not so loud: he’ll hear you” (line 31). She wants Warren to watch his words so Silas isn’t hurt. The “market things” are just groceries she sets down.
naep-r013606: Warren’s real complaint is in lines 17–18: “What help he is there’s no depending on. / Off he goes always when I need him most.” Silas leaves at haying time and comes back in winter (lines 29–30). The wages (A) are just part of their old argument; what angers Warren is being left without help.
naep-r013608: Silas thought Harold’s doubt that you could find water with a hazel prong “showed how much good school had ever done him” (line 87). He “hates to see a boy the fool of books” (line 101) and wants to teach him something practical instead: how to build a load of hay.
naep-r013612: “Haven’t to deserve” is an old way of saying “don’t have to deserve.” Warren calls home the place where “They have to take you in” (line 123); Mary offers a warmer idea—home is something you don’t have to earn. C is tempting since Silas isn’t family, but her point is about deserving, not being related.
mcas-2002-g10-q14: Jacques compares the world to a stage and people to actors. An actor enters to begin a part and exits at the end, so a person’s entrance is birth and exit is death. The speech then traces one life from “the infant” (line 5) to “mere oblivion” (line 27).
mcas-2002-g10-q15: The soldier is “sudden and quick in quarrel” (line 13)—short-tempered—and seeks “the bubble reputation / Even in the cannon’s mouth” (lines 14–15), chasing fame even into deadly danger. D is a trap: he is “Jealous in honour,” but walking into the cannon’s mouth is the opposite of cowardly.
mcas-2002-g10-q16: Treble is a high-pitched voice, like a child’s. As the old man ages, his once-deep voice turns thin and high, so it “pipes / And whistles” like a reed or a whistle. The musical words describe how his voice sounds, not instruments he plays, and nothing here mentions sleep or grandchildren.
mcas-2002-g10-q17: Oblivion is total nothingness or forgetting. Line 28 spells it out: “Sans teeth, sans eyes, sans taste, sans everything,” and sans means “without,” so being without everything is nothingness. Misery may sound fitting for old age, but these lines describe absence, not suffering.
mcas-2003-g10-q19: Almost the whole chapter describes the place: the “gloomy” prison front, the rusty “ponderous iron-work,” the “unsightly vegetation,” the wild rose-bush. No one speaks, nothing happens, and no character is developed, so the mood comes from setting. Personification shows up only in passing, as in “the deep heart of Nature.”
mcas-2003-g10-q20: Most of the chapter is grim—a prison, a cemetery, weeds. But at the prison door grows a wild rose-bush offering “fragrance and fragile beauty” to prisoners, a sign “that the deep heart of Nature could pity and be kind” (lines 34–37). The narrator even hopes it may “relieve the darkening close” of the tale.
mcas-2003-g10-q21: Near the end, the narrator speaks of “the threshold of our narrative, which is now about to issue from that inauspicious portal” (lines 45–46). A threshold is a doorway: the story is just stepping out to begin. The other quotes describe the colony, Nature, or the old jail, not where we are in the story.
mcas-2003-g10-q22: “Sad-colored garments” and “gray, steeple-crowned hats” make the scene cheerless, colorless, and grave. Nothing in these lines suggests anyone defying authority—the crowd simply stands assembled in front of the prison. That makes rebellious the one word that doesn’t fit.
mcas-2003-g10-q23: Lines 30–32 place it exactly: “on one side of the portal, and rooted almost at the threshold, was a wild rose-bush.” A portal is a doorway, so the rose grows beside the prison door. The weeds fill the grass-plot between the jail and the street; the word “But” sets the rose apart from them.
mcas-2003-g10-q24: An edifice is a large building. In line 4 the crowd stands before “a wooden edifice, the door of which was heavily timbered with oak”—the edifice has a door, so it can’t be the door. It turns out to be the prison, which line 25 calls “this ugly edifice.”
mcas-2003-g10-q25: Unsightly means unpleasant to look at—notice “sight” inside the word. The weeds are set against the rose’s “delicate gems” and “fragile beauty,” so they’re unattractive. Unhealthy is tempting, but these weeds are thriving: they find something “congenial in the soil” (line 29).
mcas-2004-g10-q15: Both stanzas open with “Life has loveliness to sell” and then list beautiful things: waves, fire, children’s faces, music, rain-wet pines, loving eyes. The call to action—“Spend all you have”—doesn’t come until stanza 3. Children appear as just one example among many, so the last choice is too narrow.
mcas-2004-g10-q16: “Soaring fire that sways and sings” gives fire human actions—swaying and singing—which is personification. There’s no “like” or “as” in line 4, so it isn’t a simile (line 6’s “like a cup” is). And “sings” isn’t a sound-imitating word, so it isn’t onomatopoeia.
mcas-2004-g10-q17: “Eyes that love you, arms that hold” describes love and a hug—the warmth people give each other. Unlike the waves and pine trees around it, this example of loveliness comes from people, not nature, which rules out surprises in nature. Nothing in the line is aggressive or unpredictable.
mcas-2004-g10-q18: Line 13, “Spend all you have for loveliness,” means pay any price for beauty, even giving up everything you have. Line 14 backs it up: “never count the cost.” The first line only says life offers beauty, and “one white singing hour of peace” names the reward, not the sacrifice.
mcas-2004-g10-q10: Paragraph 1 keeps returning to sameness: streets “very like one another,” people “equally like one another” who move “at the same hours, with the same sound upon the same pavements, to do the same work.” Even each year is “the counterpart of the last.” Efficiency may suit a factory town, but the imagery stresses monotony.
mcas-2004-g10-q11: Smoke that trails “forever and ever” and “never got uncoiled” never stops, and serpents suggest something poisonous and menacing. So the metaphor makes factory pollution an endless, harmful presence. The first choice takes the snakes literally, and the chimneys are “tall,” not crooked—it’s the smoke that coils.
mcas-2004-g10-q12: The jail, the infirmary (a hospital), and the town hall have very different purposes, yet nothing in “the graces of their construction” tells them apart—any one could pass for another. That fits the excerpt’s point about sameness. C goes too far: the sentence is about how the buildings look, not about residents getting confused.
mcas-2004-g10-q13: Nothing much happens in the excerpt, no one speaks, and no individual character appears. Every paragraph instead describes Coketown—its smoky red-and-black brick, its look-alike streets, its identical buildings—so description is the main element.
mcas-2004-g10-q14: Repeating “fact, fact, fact” in two matching halves of the sentence makes the words themselves as monotonous as the town. Dickens is criticizing Coketown, not praising it—he mocks a chapel as “a pious warehouse of red brick”—and his tone stays critical throughout, so nothing changes.
mcas-2005-g10-q37: A custom is something people do regularly, over and over. “As was their custom” (paragraph 2) tells you the young people get ready for the May-day games every year. “Weeks slipped by unnoticed” only shows how long Siegfried stayed, and the other two phrases describe the seasons.
mcas-2005-g10-q38: Flowers belong to spring’s side: the May king’s followers are “decked with evergreens and flowers,” while Old Winter is guilty “of killing the flowers.” After his defeat, a pole is decked with wild flowers and the Queen of May is crowned with violets and buttercups. Decoration is what flowers literally are, not what they symbolize.
mcas-2005-g10-q39: The fight is a game—part of “the sport” the knights were invited to join (paragraph 2). They fight with staves and willow twigs, sentence Winter “in merry sport,” and laugh throughout. Old Winter is just a role someone plays, so the choice about the two knowing each other misses the point.
mcas-2005-g10-q40: Old Winter is defeated, “doomed to a long banishment,” and then his wooden likeness is stoned, blinded, and thrown into the river. Destroying the image acts out winter’s death—hence the title, “The Many Deaths of Winter.” B confuses Winter’s crime, killing the flowers, with what the likeness stands for.
mcas-2005-g10-q19: Mrs. Bennet’s report of the ball is all about Jane: “Jane was so admired,” and Bingley “actually danced with her twice” (paragraph 12). Even her anger at Darcy comes from “his having slighted one of her daughters” (paragraph 2). She gets to the Bingley sisters’ dresses only after she has finished with Jane.
mcas-2005-g10-q20: Bingley has “easy, unaffected manners” (paragraph 1), is “lively and unreserved,” and dances every dance (paragraph 2)—the narrator calls these “amiable qualities.” He even tries to find Darcy a partner. “Unreserved” rules out shy, and all that dancing rules out lazy.
mcas-2005-g10-q21: Here report means what people were saying. The news of Darcy’s “ten thousand a year” was “in general circulation within five minutes after his entrance”—nothing was written down or researched; it simply spread from guest to guest. That’s gossip.
mcas-2005-g10-q22: Darcy’s face never changes, but the guests’ opinion of it does: talk of his income makes him “much handsomer,” and once he seems proud, he suddenly has “a most forbidding, disagreeable countenance.” Austen is mocking judgments that shallow. D is a trap—it’s Darcy’s manners that are poor, not the guests’.
mcas-2005-g10-q23: Paragraph 2 says Darcy “spent the rest of the evening in walking about the room,” and Mrs. Bennet later complains, “He walked here, and he walked there” (paragraph 16). He danced only twice and “declined being introduced” to anyone else. Sitting is what Elizabeth does, not Darcy.
mcas-2005-g10-q24: Fastidious means fussy and hard to please. Darcy has just said there’s “not another woman in the room” he could stand to dance with, and Bingley answers that he wouldn’t be so picky “for a kingdom!” B is a trap: “Upon my honour” is just an expression Bingley uses, not what fastidious means.
mcas-2005-g10-q25: Stressing me—“not handsome enough to tempt me”—implies Elizabeth might do for other men but not for someone as important as Darcy. It shows how far above the company he thinks he is. He speaks “coldly,” not angrily, so anger doesn’t fit.
mcas-2005-g10-q26: Paragraph 12 overflows with exclamations and repetition: “a most delightful evening, a most excellent ball,” “he actually danced with her twice.” She races through Bingley’s partners one by one. She is briefly “vexed” about Miss Lucas, but she’s thrilled overall; the annoyed one is Mr. Bennet, who cuts her off.
mcas-2007-g10-q14: The speaker sits through “proofs,” “figures,” and “charts and diagrams,” grows “tired and sick,” and then finds what he needs looking up “in perfect silence at the stars.” Measuring the stars can’t match the wonder of seeing them. B is close, but the poem is about wonder, not recreation, and D is far too literal.
mcas-2007-g10-q15: The speaker grows “tired and sick” while hearing a lecture full of numbers and charts, and the feeling ends as soon as he slips outside. He’s fed up with the lecture, not physically ill. Even “unaccountable” suggests a mood he can’t quite explain, not a disease.
mcas-2007-g10-q16: The lecture room is full of talk and “much applause” (line 4). The “perfect silence” under the stars sets up a contrast: noise and numbers inside, quiet wonder outside. B misreads the mood—he chose to wander off by himself, and the ending feels peaceful, not lonely.
mcas-2007-g10-q17: In lines 6–8 the speaker leaves the lecture, wanders off “by myself” into the “mystical moist night air,” and looks at the stars on his own. The poem values experiencing nature firsthand over hearing it explained. Learning about astronomy is exactly what he walks away from.
mcas-2007-g10-q18: “Learn’d” is an old spelling of the adjective “learned,” which means highly educated. The astronomer is an expert presenting “proofs” and “figures” to “much applause,” so knowledgeable fits. Remembered is the trap—it reads the word as the past tense of “learn.”
mcas-2023-g8-q13: In paragraph 5 the narrator feels “the purest gratitude” because his skin has “begun to blister and peel off.” A painful sunburn is something most people would hate, but he loves it because it gives him the weather-beaten look of an old traveler. That gap between the situation and his reaction is the irony.
mcas-2023-g8-q14: Twain never becomes a pilot—his hope “struggled to a reluctant death” (paragraph 3)—and his Amazon plan is half-baked. Yet once the boat sails, he becomes “a new being,” thrilled just to be “a traveler!” (paragraph 4). C is tempting, but his showing off never actually leads to embarrassment in the passage.
mcas-2024-g10-q10: The road seems to plead, “Venture not—if you leave me you are lost,” and calls itself “well-beaten,” the safe, familiar path (lines 9–12). The speaker answers, “I am not afraid to leave you, yet I love you” (lines 13–14). He loves what he knows but is ready to go beyond it.
mcas-2024-g10-q11: In lines 18–24, “I think” introduces hopes and beliefs. By lines 43–47, “I will recruit,” “I will scatter,” and “I will toss” turn those feelings into firm promises, showing his commitment growing. C overstates it: saying “I will” shows determination, not proof that he can carry out his plans.
mcas-2024-g10-q12: To “grow in the open air” and “eat and sleep with the earth” means living immersed in nature. Throughout the poem, life on the open road helps the speaker discover himself: “I am larger, better than I thought” (line 37). B is tempting since he praises freedom, but these lines credit the earth, not independence.
mcas-2025-g10-q1: Luxuriant sits in a list of signs of rich growth—“green pastures,” an “abundance of flowers,” and “a generous harvest”—all set against “dust-covered desolation.” It means growing thickly and richly, so flourishing fits. Mature means fully grown, which misses the idea of lushness.
mcas-2025-g10-q2: Handkerchiefs over faces and vaseline in nostrils are steps you’d take only if the dust hurt to breathe. Later in paragraph 2 she tries “to avoid inhaling the irritating dust,” and in paragraph 10 it worsens Will’s “bronchial trouble.” Nothing mentions stained clothing, and her efforts are “almost hopeless,” not productive.
